evidence.claim: Highway 12 turns south from Santa Rosa into Sonoma Valley, passing Glen Ellen on its way to Sonoma.
evidence.quote: After passing east through Santa Rosa on a mix of freeway, surface street, and expressway, it turns south into the Sonoma Valley, passing the Jack London State Historic Park at Glen Ellen. It winds through Sonoma on surface streets

evidence.claim: The valley lies between the Mayacamas and Sonoma mountains, with Sonoma Creek flowing toward San Pablo Bay.
evidence.quote: The valley is located in southeastern Sonoma County between the Mayacamas Mountains and Sonoma Mountains. It stretches from San Pablo Bay in the south to the city of Santa Rosa in the north. Sonoma Creek flows down the valley to the bay.

evidence.claim: The officially designated State Scenic Highway segment runs from Danielli Avenue east of Santa Rosa to London Way near Agua Caliente.
evidence.quote: it is only designated as a scenic highway from its intersection with Danielli Avenue east of Santa Rosa to its junction with London Way near Agua Caliente

evidence.claim: The road could have taken a different form at the Santa Rosa end.
evidence.quote: Beginning in the 1950s, land was purchased by the California Department of Transportation to build a freeway alignment for California State Route 12 through eastern Santa Rosa.

evidence.claim: Beginning in the 1950s, the California Department of Transportation bought land for a freeway alignment through eastern Santa Rosa.
evidence.quote: Beginning in the 1950s, land was purchased by the California Department of Transportation to build a freeway alignment for California State Route 12 through eastern Santa Rosa.

evidence.claim: The city later purchased that land for a two-mile pedestrian and bicycle path linking the freeway’s eastern end with Spring Lake Regional Park.
evidence.quote: the city purchased the land to build a 2-mile (3.2 km) pedestrian and bicycle path from the eastern end of the route 12 freeway to Spring Lake Regional Park.

evidence.claim: Heading south, reach Kenwood between Bennett Mountain to the west and Sugarloaf Ridge to the northeast, in an area of vineyards and wineries.
evidence.quote: Bennett Mountain lies west of the town, and Sugarloaf Ridge to the northeast.

evidence.claim: Sonoma Creek runs through Glen Ellen, where Jack London’s former ranch is now a state historic park.
evidence.quote: Sonoma Creek, the principal river of the Sonoma Valley, flows through Glen Ellen.

evidence.claim: Beyond Glen Ellen, Agua Caliente and Fetters Hot Springs lie along Sonoma Highway northwest of Sonoma.
evidence.quote: Fetters Hot Springs and Agua Caliente are adjacent communities located along the Sonoma Highway (State Route 12), approximately 2.5 miles (4.0 km) northwest of Sonoma

evidence.claim: Continue beyond the designated segment into Sonoma, where Highway 12 winds along surface streets past the historic park’s mission and Vallejo Estate.
evidence.quote: It winds through Sonoma on surface streets, where the historic Vallejo Estate and Sonoma Mission, both part of the Sonoma State Historic Park, are.

evidence.claim: Kenwood grew from a town laid out with a railway in mind.
evidence.quote: In 1887, the Sonoma Land & Improvement Company, which owned the property on which the town now sits, laid out lots in anticipation of the railroad

evidence.claim: The Sonoma Land & Improvement Company divided the property into lots in 1887; the community went through the names Rohrerville, Los Guilicos and South Los Guilicos.
evidence.quote: In 1887, the Sonoma Land & Improvement Company, which owned the property on which the town now sits, laid out lots in anticipation of the railroad which would arrive the following year. The infant community tried on many names: Rohrerville, for one of the owners of the land company; Los Guilicos, and then South Los Guilicos, for the Mexican land grant.

evidence.claim: Around 1895, residents voted to change the name after complaints that Guilicos was hard to pronounce.
evidence.quote: A number of townspeople were unhappy, complaining that "Guilicos" was hard to pronounce. Around 1895 a vote was taken to change the name again.

evidence.claim: The railway’s stone depot became a community center after Southern Pacific sold it to the Kenwood Improvement Club in 1940.
evidence.quote: In 1940, Southern Pacific sold the depot to the Kenwood Improvement Club for $500 (equivalent to $11,490 in 2025) and it was converted into a community center.

evidence.claim: Rail service ended in 1936, and the tracks were removed in 1942.
evidence.quote: Rail service continued until 1936, and the rail line was removed in 1942.

evidence.claim: A vineyard gave Glen Ellen its name.
evidence.quote: eventually establishing a 1,000-acre (4.0 km2) vineyard he named Glen Ellen after his wife.  The town that grew up around the vineyard also came to be called Glen Ellen

evidence.claim: Charles V. Stuart established a 1,000-acre vineyard and named it for his wife; the town that developed beside it adopted the same name.
evidence.quote: eventually establishing a 1,000-acre (4.0 km2) vineyard he named Glen Ellen after his wife.  The town that grew up around the vineyard also came to be called Glen Ellen

evidence.claim: His home was later renamed Glen Oaks Ranch.
evidence.quote: Stuart's home was later renamed Glen Oaks Ranch.

evidence.claim: Jack London lived in Glen Ellen from 1909 until his death in 1916, working on Beauty Ranch and Wolf House.
evidence.quote: Writer Jack London lived in Glen Ellen from 1909 to his death in 1916, where he devoted much of his time to development of his Beauty Ranch and the building of his mansion, Wolf House.

evidence.claim: Glen Ellen and Sonoma County also entered his fiction, including The Iron Heel and The Valley of the Moon.
evidence.quote: Many of his novels and stories, notably The Iron Heel and The Valley of the Moon mention Glen Ellen and Sonoma County.

evidence.claim: Sonoma Creek, the valley’s principal river, flows through town.
evidence.quote: Sonoma Creek, the principal river of the Sonoma Valley, flows through Glen Ellen.

evidence.claim: Wolf House survives as stone ruins on the eastern slope of Sonoma Mountain.
evidence.quote: The Jack London home, called the Wolf House, is a sizable stone structure, which was destroyed by fire and whose ruins are visible within the state park property.

evidence.claim: Construction began in 1910, but the house burned on August 22, 1913, before Jack and Charmian London could move in.
evidence.quote: Construction on the 15,000 square foot (1,393 square meters) house began in 1910.

evidence.claim: The couple pledged to rebuild, and workers began drying redwood logs for the project.
evidence.quote: They pledged to rebuild the house and workers began drying redwood logs in preparation.

evidence.claim: London died in 1916 before the wood was ready, and construction stopped.
evidence.quote: he died in 1916 before the wood was ready. Construction halted with his death.

evidence.claim: Another house tells Charmian’s part of the story: the House of Happy Walls now serves as the park’s visitor center and museum.
evidence.quote: Today the building serves as the visitor center and a museum for Jack London State Historic Park.

evidence.claim: Much of its furniture had been intended for Wolf House.
evidence.quote: much of its furniture was originally intended for use in the Wolf House.

evidence.claim: The stone ruins of Wolf House remain visible within the park.
evidence.quote: The Jack London home, called the Wolf House, is a sizable stone structure, which was destroyed by fire and whose ruins are visible within the state park property.
